questions.question: In which EC2 instance state does AWS charge for compute resources?

options.text: Pending
Running
Stopped
Hibernating

explanation.correct: AWS charges EC2 compute costs only while the instance is in the Running state.
explanation.why: A (Pending) is a transition state — no charge. C (Stopped) — compute stops, only EBS is charged. D (Hibernating) — same as stopped, only EBS storage is charged.

questions.question: What happens to the EBS storage attached to an EC2 instance when the instance is stopped?

options.text: It is deleted automatically
It is detached and returned to AWS
It remains attached and AWS continues to charge for it
It is compressed to save cost

explanation.correct: EBS storage remains allocated to the instance even in the stopped state, and AWS charges for the storage consumed.
explanation.why: A, B, D are all incorrect — the EBS volume stays intact and attached. Only termination (by default) removes the root EBS volume.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes vertical scaling?

options.text: Adding more EC2 instances to handle increased load
Changing the instance type of an existing EC2 instance to a larger or smaller type
Distributing traffic across multiple instances using a load balancer
Automatically launching new instances based on demand

explanation.correct: Vertical scaling means resizing the existing instance — increasing or decreasing its CPU and RAM by changing the instance type.
explanation.why: A describes horizontal scaling (scale out). C describes load balancing. D describes Auto Scaling. All are horizontal strategies.

questions.question: What is the term for adding more EC2 instances to handle increased traffic?

options.text: Scale Up
Scale Down
Scale Out
Scale In

explanation.correct: Scale Out means adding more instances horizontally. It is a form of horizontal scaling.
explanation.why: Scale Up = increase existing instance size (vertical). Scale Down = decrease existing instance size (vertical). Scale In = remove instances (horizontal — reducing).

questions.question: What is the default shutdown behavior of an EC2 instance?

options.text: Terminate
Reboot
Hibernate
Stop

explanation.correct: The default shutdown behavior is Stop — the instance enters the stopped state and can be restarted.
explanation.why: Terminate would delete the instance permanently — too dangerous as a default. Reboot and Hibernate are separate actions, not the shutdown behavior default.

questions.question: You have enabled Termination Protection on an EC2 instance. A teammate clicks Terminate. What happens?

options.text: The instance is terminated after a 5-minute delay
AWS sends an email confirmation before proceeding
The terminate action fails with an error
The instance enters shutting-down state but is restored automatically

explanation.correct: With Termination Protection enabled, the terminate action is blocked immediately and returns an error. The instance is completely unaffected.
explanation.why: There is no delay, no email, no automatic restore. The protection simply prevents the action from executing.

questions.question: Which EC2 instance states incur EBS storage charges? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Running
Stopped
Hibernating
Terminated

explanation.correct: Running, Stopped, and Hibernating all incur EBS storage charges because the volume remains allocated. Terminated does not — the root volume is deleted.
explanation.why: The question is about EBS only. Running charges both compute AND EBS. Stopped and Hibernating charge only EBS. Terminated = no charges.

questions.question: What is the key difference between stopping and terminating an EC2 instance?

options.text: Stopping is faster than terminating
Stopping preserves the instance and its data; termination permanently deletes the instance
Termination preserves EBS data while stopping deletes it
Stopping requires the instance to be in a specific region

explanation.correct: Stop = shut down, data preserved, can restart. Terminate = permanent deletion, instance and root EBS volume gone, cannot recover.
explanation.why: Speed is irrelevant. C has it backwards. D is false — stop works in any region.

questions.question: What must you do BEFORE changing the instance type of a running EC2 instance (standard resize)?

options.text: Create a new AMI snapshot
Detach all EBS volumes
Stop the instance
Terminate the instance

explanation.correct: Standard instance type changes require the instance to be in the Stopped state first. The instance must be stopped before you can change its type.
explanation.why: A is not required (though recommended before major changes). B would cause data loss risk. D is irreversible — you cannot resize a terminated instance.

questions.question: What does EC2 hibernation save to EBS before pausing the instance?

options.text: CPU register contents
The RAM (memory) contents
Application log files
The network configuration

explanation.correct: Hibernation saves the entire RAM contents (memory dump) to the EBS root volume. This allows the instance to resume exactly from where it paused.
explanation.why: CPU registers, logs, and network config are not what enables the resume-from-state behavior. The RAM dump is what captures the complete running state.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has Stop Protection ENABLED and Shutdown Behavior set to STOP. An admin runs sudo shutdown now from inside the OS. What happens?

options.text: The instance stops normally
The instance is terminated
The instance remains in the Running state
The instance enters the Stopping state then recovers to Running

explanation.correct: Stop Protection takes the upper hand. Even though Shutdown Behavior says to stop, and even though the OS issued a shutdown, the protection prevents the stop. The instance remains running.
explanation.why: A would be correct if Stop Protection were disabled. B would require Terminate shutdown behavior AND no Termination Protection. D is not a real state sequence.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of vertical scaling compared to horizontal scaling?

options.text: Vertical scaling is more expensive
Vertical scaling requires downtime because the instance must be stopped
Vertical scaling permanently deletes the instance
Vertical scaling is not supported on T-family instances

explanation.correct: Vertical scaling requires stopping the EC2 instance, which causes downtime. Applications are unreachable during the resize. Horizontal scaling does not require stopping existing instances.
explanation.why: Cost depends on instance type — not inherently more expensive. It does not delete anything. T-family instances do support resizing.

questions.question: After a stop-start cycle (not a reboot), which of the following changes for an EC2 instance?

options.text: The instance ID
The EBS volume data
The public IP address (if no Elastic IP is assigned)
The security group assignment

explanation.correct: When an instance is stopped and started, it may launch on a different physical host. Unless an Elastic IP is assigned, the public IP address changes.
explanation.why: The Instance ID never changes. EBS data is persistent through stop-start. Security groups remain associated unless manually changed.

questions.question: What does scale-in mean in the context of horizontal scaling?

options.text: Reducing the CPU and RAM of an existing instance
Adding more instances to handle increased load
Removing instances when load decreases
Terminating all instances in a region

explanation.correct: Scale-in means removing (terminating) instances as load decreases, reducing the fleet size. It is the opposite of scale-out.
explanation.why: A describes scale-down (vertical). B describes scale-out. D is not a standard scaling operation.

questions.question: You need to change a running T3.medium EC2 to a C5.large (different instance family). Which statement is correct?

options.text: This can be done live using the Nitro hot-resize feature
This requires stopping the instance first
This is not possible — you must launch a new instance
This is only possible if Termination Protection is disabled

explanation.correct: Changing between different instance families (T to C) requires stopping the instance. Live resizing (Nitro hot-resize) currently applies only within the same instance family.
explanation.why: A applies only within-family Nitro instances. C is wrong — cross-family resizing is possible with a stop. D is unrelated to Termination Protection.

questions.question: Which AWS service can be used to monitor EC2 CPU and memory metrics?

options.text: AWS Config
CloudWatch
CloudTrail
AWS Inspector

explanation.correct: Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service. It collects CPU, network, and disk metrics from EC2. With the CloudWatch agent installed, you can also monitor memory and application-level metrics.
explanation.why: Config tracks configuration changes. CloudTrail tracks API calls. Inspector checks for security vulnerabilities.

questions.question: AWS charges for data transfer in which direction?

options.text: Data transfer INTO AWS (inbound)
Data transfer OUT from AWS (outbound)
Both inbound and outbound equally
Only between regions, not to the internet

explanation.correct: AWS charges for data transfer OUT (from AWS to the internet / other regions). Data transfer IN to AWS is free.
explanation.why: A is wrong — inbound is free. C is wrong. D is partially true for inter-region transfer but the main principle is outbound is charged.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has been in the Stopped state for 30 days. What charges has the owner incurred?

options.text: No charges at all
Full EC2 compute charges for 30 days
EBS storage charges for 30 days
Both compute and EBS charges for 30 days

explanation.correct: In the Stopped state, compute charges stop but the EBS volume remains allocated. AWS charges for the EBS storage consumed over those 30 days.
explanation.why: A is wrong — storage is still charged. B is wrong — no compute in stopped state. D is wrong — compute is not charged when stopped.

questions.question: What is the AWS Nitro System?

options.text: A database optimization tool
AWS's modern virtualization platform used in EC2 data centers
A network security filtering service
An automated backup service for EBS volumes

explanation.correct: The AWS Nitro System is AWS's modern hypervisor and virtualization platform. It offloads virtualization functions to dedicated hardware, improving performance. It also enables advanced features like live resizing.
explanation.why: It is not a database tool, security filter, or backup service. It is the underlying compute virtualization infrastructure.

questions.question: Which is NOT a valid state in the EC2 instance lifecycle?

options.text: Pending
Rebooting
Suspended
Hibernating

explanation.correct: Suspended is not a valid EC2 instance state. The valid states are: Pending, Running, Stopping, Stopped, Rebooting, Hibernating, Shutting-down, and Terminated.
explanation.why: A, B, D are all real EC2 states. C (Suspended) is not part of the EC2 instance lifecycle.

questions.question: A company needs to resize a critical production EC2 instance with zero downtime. What is the most appropriate strategy?

options.text: Stop the instance, change type, start it back up
Enable Termination Protection before resizing
Use Blue-Green Deployment — launch a pre-sized instance, redirect traffic, decommission old
Hibernating the instance before resizing

explanation.correct: Blue-Green Deployment launches a new, correctly-sized instance while the original runs. Traffic is shifted to the new instance via a load balancer. Once verified, the old instance is removed — zero downtime.
explanation.why: A causes downtime (must stop). B prevents termination but does not solve downtime. D — hibernating pauses the instance but you still cannot resize a hibernating instance.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has Termination Protection ENABLED and Shutdown Behavior set to TERMINATE. A developer runs sudo shutdown now from inside the OS. What is the result?

options.text: The instance is terminated
The instance stops (Stopped state)
The instance remains running — protection wins over shutdown behavior
The instance hibernates

explanation.correct: When Shutdown Behavior is Terminate but Termination Protection is enabled, the protection takes the upper hand. The terminate action is blocked and the instance remains running.
explanation.why: A would happen if protection were disabled. B would happen if shutdown behavior were Stop (not Terminate). D is unrelated to this scenario.

questions.question: What is the minimum requirement for EC2 hibernation to work?

options.text: The instance must have at least 4 GB of RAM
The root EBS volume must be encrypted and large enough to hold the RAM contents
The instance must be in a stopped state before hibernation is triggered
Hibernation must be enabled after launch via Instance Settings

explanation.correct: For hibernation to work, the root EBS volume must be encrypted (the RAM dump contains sensitive data) and must have enough free space to store the entire RAM contents.
explanation.why: A — there is no fixed 4 GB minimum; it depends on instance size. C — you hibernate a running instance, not a stopped one. D — hibernation must be enabled at launch time, not after.

questions.question: A T3.micro instance ran for 18 hours, was stopped for 6 hours, then terminated. Approximately what is billed?

options.text: 24 hours of compute + 24 hours of EBS
18 hours of compute + 24 hours of EBS
18 hours of compute + 18 hours of EBS
24 hours of compute + 18 hours of EBS

explanation.correct: Compute charges: 18 hours (running only). EBS charges: 24 hours total — EBS is charged for the full duration the volume was provisioned, including when stopped.
explanation.why: AWS does not charge compute during the 6 stopped hours. But the EBS volume existed and was allocated for all 24 hours, so EBS is charged for the full 24 hours.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between Shutdown Behavior and Stop/Termination Protection?

options.text: Shutdown Behavior always overrides Protection settings
Protection settings always take precedence over Shutdown Behavior
They operate independently and cannot conflict
Shutdown Behavior only applies when Protection is disabled

explanation.correct: Protection settings (Stop Protection and Termination Protection) take precedence over Shutdown Behavior. If protection prevents an action, even the OS-level shutdown cannot complete it.
explanation.why: A has it backwards. C is wrong — they can and do conflict. D is wrong — Shutdown Behavior always exists, protection just blocks its outcome.

questions.question: What is the difference between rebooting and performing a stop then start on an EC2 instance?

options.text: Reboot changes the instance type; stop-start preserves it
Reboot keeps the instance on the same host; stop-start may move it to a different host
Stop-start is faster than a reboot
Reboot causes EBS data loss; stop-start does not

explanation.correct: During a reboot, the instance stays on the same physical host — public IP is preserved. During stop-start, the instance may be placed on a different physical host — and the public IP changes unless an Elastic IP is assigned.
explanation.why: A is wrong — neither changes instance type. C is wrong — stop-start is typically slower. D is wrong — both preserve EBS data.

questions.question: A developer reports that their application on EC2 is running slowly. The CloudWatch metrics show CPU utilization at 95% consistently. You have a T3.micro. What is the MOST appropriate first response?

options.text: Terminate and relaunch with a T3.medium
Stop the instance, change to T3.medium, and restart
Add a second T3.micro instance (horizontal scaling)
Enable hibernation to free up CPU

explanation.correct: For a single dev server with a CPU bottleneck, vertical scaling (stop, change to T3.medium, restart) is the most straightforward response. It is a dev environment so downtime is acceptable.
explanation.why: A (terminate) would destroy data. C is valid for production but adds complexity for a simple dev fix. D — hibernation frees nothing; it pauses the instance entirely.

questions.question: EC2 pricing varies based on which factors? (Choose all correct)

options.text: Instance type (CPU/RAM size)
Operating system (Linux vs Windows)
AWS Region
The number of users accessing the instance

explanation.correct: EC2 pricing varies by instance type, operating system, and AWS region. Linux instances cost less than Windows (due to licensing). US-East regions are typically cheaper than Asia Pacific.
explanation.why: D is wrong — AWS does not charge based on user count or traffic volume for EC2 compute. A, B, and C are all real pricing dimensions.

questions.question: You terminate an EC2 instance. Which of the following correctly describes what happens to the root EBS volume?

options.text: It is detached and kept, incurring storage charges
It is deleted by default
It is converted to a snapshot automatically
It is transferred to S3

explanation.correct: By default, the root EBS volume is deleted when the EC2 instance is terminated (Delete on Termination = true by default). Additional data volumes are not deleted by default.
explanation.why: A is the behavior for non-root volumes unless configured otherwise. C and D do not happen automatically. This is an important exam distinction.

questions.question: What is the most cost-effective way to run a dev server that is only needed 8 hours per weekday?

options.text: Run it 24/7 to avoid stop-start overhead
Stop it when not in use — pay only for 8 hours/day of compute
Hibernate it when not in use to eliminate all charges
Use Termination Protection to freeze costs

explanation.correct: Stopping the instance when not in use means you only pay for 8 hours of compute per weekday instead of 24. EBS storage still incurs a small charge, but this is far cheaper than running 24/7.
explanation.why: A wastes money. C — hibernation still charges EBS and does not eliminate charges. D — Termination Protection has nothing to do with billing costs.
